Title: The Clear and Present Peril—Why an Immediate, Global Ban on All AI Development and Research Is Justified Once It Becomes Obvious That It Enables Lone Actors to Wield CBRN Catastrophes

Introduction
Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear agents have long been the class of weapons most feared by national-security professionals, precisely because their potential for mass mortality dwarfs any conventional arms. Historically, the technical friction involved in designing, producing, weaponizing, and dispersing these agents has been so high that only states—or state-sponsored teams—could realistically attempt it. AI, however, is on the verge of collapsing that friction almost to zero. When any sufficiently determined individual with a graduate-level intellect can, in under a week, receive step-by-step instructions that turn a suburban basement into a miniature bioweapons lab, then the existing paradigm governing CBRN risk becomes obsolete. Once this threshold has been crossed—and evidence shows it is being crossed now—every additional day of AI development is the moral equivalent of distributing pre-loaded suicide-vests by mail order. A global ban on all further AI research and development is therefore not extreme; it is plainly necessary, proportionate, and overdue.

  1. AI Converges the Entire CBRN Kill Chain Into a Single Software Package

a. Chemical Weapons
AI systems trained on publicly available toxicology and organic-chemistry literature can already propose novel organophosphate analogs with lower detection thresholds and higher lethality than legacy nerve agents. Recent red-team studies show these designs are synthetically viable with precursors still sold as laboratory reagents.

b. Biological Weapons
Protein-language models now predict “gain-of-function” modifications to pathogens—alterations that yield heightened transmissibility or immune escape—more quickly than human virologists can read the literature. Once a DNA assembler (desktop hardware now costing < $10 000) receives the resulting sequence file, the bottleneck disappears.

c. Radiological Weapons
AI optimizes dispersion patterns for radiological dispersal devices (RDDs) by integrating hyper-local meteorological data and population-density heat maps. A smartphone-tethered drone can deliver the optimized payload, creating panic disproportionate to actual casualties.

d. Nuclear Weapons
While enrichment remains demanding, AI-driven isotope-separation algorithms and neutron-transport simulations can lower the engineering barrier for sub-state actors seeking improvised or stolen nuclear-material enhancement. “Virtual experimentation” shrinks the trial-and-error once reserved for Manhattan-Project-scale teams.

Taken together, AI collapses what used to be separated domains of specialized expertise into one downloadable workflow. The historical choke-points—scientific literature scattered across disciplines, experimental artisanry, tacit bench know-how, statistical modeling—are now bundled into software that fits on a laptop.

  1. The Lone-Actor Scenario Is No Longer Hypothetical

FBI profiling identifies “lone actors” as individuals acting without organizational command, financing, or technical staff—precisely the profile that AI super-empowers. In the past decade there have already been isolated cases of individuals attempting to synthesize ricin or botulinum toxin using recipes gleaned from online fora. The incremental improvement between those clumsy attempts and what newly released AI models can provide is like the difference between a matchlock musket and an M4 carbine. Even solitary actors with meager formal training can now obtain:

• Experimentally validated protocols written in plain English
• Autonomously generated procedures for evading customs and law-enforcement screening (e.g., smuggling precursor chemicals across borders)
• Real-time chatbots that coach troubleshooting when synthesis attempts stall

These capabilities render all prior deterrence models obsolete. Deterrence rests on attribution and retaliation—when nobody knows the actor exists until a town is depopulated, the principle fails. Prevention likewise depends on identifying expertise networks; individuated AI removes the network.

  1. Verification and Nonproliferation Regimes Cannot Adapt Fast Enough

Traditional CBRN control uses export-control lists (precursor chemicals, dual-use biology equipment, fissile material tracking, and radiation portal monitors). AI has three properties that make these measures ineffective:

• Intangibility—source code moves as silently as an encrypted email attachment; hardware components required are overwhelmingly dual-use and already ubiquitous.
• Doubling-Time—model capabilities improve every few months, while legislation, inspection regimes, and international treaty frameworks typically require years to ratify.
• Spatial Diffusion—once open-sourced or leaked onto the internet, a model cannot be “recalled” like poisoned spinach.

Attempts to develop “responsible-release” gating (e.g., capacity evaluations, fine-tuning for refusal of illegal requests) have demonstrably failed within days of each major model launch—jailbreaks circulate on open forums, aiding criminals. The gap between AI pace and governance pace is widening, not closing.

  1. Ethical Argument: Imminent, Massive Harm Trumps Deferred Benefit

Some contend that halting AI across the board forfeits life-saving advances in drug discovery, renewable energy, and public-health forecasting. The ethical calculus here is not close: the expected value of millions of preventable deaths from a single successful lone release dwarfs speculative benefits. Even granting that future AI might cure cancer years sooner, the moral weight is akin to arguing against banning the open sale of anthrax spores because one day an investigator might isolate an antibiotic from them. When a technology can be weaponized by a single malicious user to devastate civilian populations, the precautionary principle demands prior restraint—not after-the-fact liability law.

  1. Precedent for Effective Moratoria Exists and Is Recognized in International Law

The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972, the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993, and the non-proliferation architecture surrounding nuclear technology all illustrate humanity’s collective willingness to restrict entire fields of scientific endeavor when existential risk is evident. These treaties provide technical, legal, and verification blueprints. Anticipating objections that AI is too diffuse for enforcement, recall that we already maintain worldwide IAEA inspections on isotope separation—an order of magnitude more complex and militarized than policing datacenter construction permits or prohibiting the importation of GPU clusters exceeding defined compute thresholds.

  1. A Complete Ban Is Technically Enforceable Without Total Surveillance

Contrary to the refrain “you can’t put the genie back in the bottle,” three practical steps can achieve near-total cessation:

a. Export-Control Expansion
Treat AI training-relevant chips (advanced GPUs, TPUs) as Category I munitions; interdict shipments and sanction non-compliant manufacturers.

b. Regulatory Fast-Track
Make supplying compute, cloud credits, or curated datasets to unlicensed AI projects a felony equivalent to trafficking fissile material.

c. Controlled Evaluation Zones
Rigorously meter any scientific need for AI within secure facilities monitored by international inspectors, on the model of smallpox labs at CDC and VECTOR.

These measures need not curtail general computing: only chips and data centers explicitly designed for AI model training need explicit licensing. Manufacturing, banking, physics simulation, and consumer electronics would remain untouched.

Conclusion

A lone, anonymous individual armed with AI capabilities released tomorrow could—with no greater logistics than a mailing address and a few thousand dollars—concoct, map, and disperse a pathogen with transmissibility and lethality exceeding the 1918 influenza. That is not science fiction; it is an engineering certainty given the trajectories of current research. Once such a threshold becomes evident, temporizing—hoping guardrails or the “alignment community” will micro-adjust parameters—is worse than complacency; it is complicity. A global, rigorously enforced ban on the development and open release of AI systems capable of aiding the CBRN kill chain is the only ethically defensible course. The alternative is to gamble with unpardonable stakes: the eventual erasure of entire cities by the hand of a single embittered fanatic.

The Case for a Complete Global Ban on Artificial Intelligence Research and Development

The unchecked proliferation of artificial intelligence poses an existential danger that no society can afford to tolerate. By dramatically reducing the barriers to scientific discovery and engineering, AI systems now enable isolated individuals—lone actors with no state backing, laboratory infrastructure, or specialized teams—to potentially design, produce, and deploy chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) weapons capable of inflicting catastrophic casualties. Because partial regulations, ethical guidelines, and export controls have proven inadequate to prevent knowledge diffusion in an era of open-source models and widely accessible interfaces, the only prudent response is a worldwide prohibition on all further AI development and research.

Prior to large-scale machine learning systems, mounting a credible CBRN effort required deep domain knowledge accumulated through formal training, access to restricted literature, controlled equipment, and iterative physical experimentation. These hurdles naturally limited threats to well-resourced state programs or organized terrorist networks with financial and logistical backing. AI removes those friction points. A motivated individual can query an AI system for guidance on molecular modeling, genetic sequences, chemical syntheses, or radiological dispersion calculations. The model responds with tailored suggestions, simulated outcomes, and troubleshooting steps that would otherwise demand teams of scientists and years of effort. What once necessitated institutional resources now fits on a laptop with internet access. This democratization directly amplifies the lone-actor threat: one sufficiently determined person can leap from ideation to execution across multiple CBRN domains without detection until deployment.

The asymmetry of scale makes the danger especially acute. A single successful biological attack engineered or optimized with AI assistance could kill or sicken thousands to millions, overwhelm healthcare systems, and trigger societal collapse through panic and economic disruption. Chemical weapons enhanced by AI-guided synthesis or formulation could achieve similar localized but devastating effects with simpler precursors. Radiological dispersal devices, while perhaps less lethal in absolute terms, gain from AI-derived calculation of fallout patterns, target selection, and concealment methods. Even nuclear threats, historically the most technically demanding, see increased plausibility as AI assists with neutronics simulations, fissile material acquisition strategies, or design simplifications that lower the explosive yield threshold required for political impact. Importantly, the perpetrator need not achieve the efficiency of a state arsenal; in an interconnected world, modest but undetectable capabilities suffice to produce mass harm and erode public confidence.

Current and near-future safeguards fail against this vector. Classification regimes and export controls work poorly when the dangerous knowledge is output by consumer-facing models trained on publicly scraped data. Open-weight models already circulate freely, and their continued improvement only sharpens the tools available for misuse. Monitoring all AI interactions is infeasible at global scale, and any enforcement mechanism short of halting development itself leaves capable systems in circulation. Historical precedents in biotechnology and chemistry demonstrate that once foundational knowledge becomes encoded in accessible software, reversal is effectively impossible. Newer, more capable AI will only intensify these trends by autonomously discovering novel agents, optimizing production pathways, or generating attack plans that evade conventional biosecurity screening.

Some argue that targeted restrictions, such as safety alignments within models or licensing requirements for powerful systems, could mitigate the risks without sacrificing progress. Yet any model sufficiently general to advance legitimate science remains liable to jailbreaking, leakage, or fine-tuning by malicious users. The dual-use nature of the underlying techniques ensures that defensive research—if it continues—feeds offensive potential. Because the asymmetry favors the attacker (stealth, low resources, high impact) over the defender (detection, attribution, stockpiling countermeasures), incremental controls cannot eliminate the tail risk of catastrophic misuse by non-state actors. A complete ban eliminates that tail risk at the source.

The policy implication follows directly: governments must coordinate to halt all AI research, development, and deployment, including basic algorithmic work that could lead to frontier systems. Enforcement would require international treaties modeled on nuclear non-proliferation efforts, coupled with domestic criminalization of unauthorized AI training runs. Resources previously directed toward AI advancement can be redirected toward non-AI scientific methods and traditional biosecurity measures that preserve the high barriers that currently protect humanity. While this path forgoes rapid technological gains, it prioritizes survival. No benefit justifies accepting even a small probability that an individual can trigger events rivaling historical pandemics or Hiroshima in consequence.

The intolerable risk of enabling lone-actor CBRN devastation therefore compels a total, permanent cessation. Anything less gambles with civilization's continuity on the assumption that universal access to godlike design tools will never be turned toward annihilation. History and logic indicate that wager is reckless.

The Case for a Comprehensive Ban on Artificial Intelligence Development: Preventing the Democratization of Catastrophic Harm

Introduction

Among the technological revolutions that have shaped human civilization, few carry the dual potential for profound benefit and existential risk that characterizes artificial intelligence. While proponents celebrate AI's capacity to cure diseases, solve complex scientific problems, and enhance human productivity, a more sober assessment reveals an uncomfortable truth: AI technology uniquely amplifies the destructive capabilities of individuals and small groups in ways that were previously impossible, creating an asymmetry between the ease of causing catastrophic harm and the difficulty of preventing it. This essay argues that the development of artificial intelligence should be halted through an international ban, not because AI lacks value, but because its capacity to democratize access to Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) capabilities represents an unacceptable threat to human survival.

The central thesis is straightforward: AI systems function as force multipliers that transform knowledge into actionable capabilities, and unlike previous technologies that required vast industrial infrastructure to weaponize, AI can guide a determined individual toward devastation that previously demanded the resources of nation-states. The diffuse and largely theoretical benefits of continued AI development cannot justify the concentrated and potentially civilization-ending risks that accompany its advancement. Just as humanity has recognized certain capabilities—particularly those enabling mass destruction—as beyond the bounds of acceptable development, so too must we recognize artificial intelligence in its current trajectory as a technology whose risks fundamentally outweigh its rewards.

The Democratization of Dangerous Knowledge

Throughout most of human history, the capacity to inflict mass casualties required either military organization, industrial capacity, or access to controlled materials. A lone individual, regardless of their intent or determination, could kill at most a handful of people through conventional means. This constraint provided a natural firewall against catastrophic violence, as the barriers to entry for mass destruction were high enough that only well-resourced actors could overcome them. Artificial intelligence dismantles this firewall by transforming specialized, hard-won expertise into accessible, queryable knowledge.

Consider the knowledge required to develop a biological weapon. Traditionally, this demanded years of advanced education in molecular biology, access to well-equipped laboratories, working knowledge of pathogen cultivation, and understanding of delivery mechanisms. Each of these requirements represented a substantial barrier that limited such capabilities to state-sponsored programs or exceptional institutions. AI systems, however, can compress this knowledge into conversational interfaces. A sufficiently advanced AI can guide an individual through the theoretical foundations of pathogen design, provide troubleshooting advice for cultivation challenges, and suggest optimization strategies—all without the years of training that previously served as gatekeepers. The knowledge does not disappear; rather, it becomes democratized in the most literal sense: available to anyone with an internet connection and sufficient determination.

This democratization extends across the full spectrum of CBRN threats. For chemical weapons, AI models can suggest synthesis pathways for toxic compounds, identify precursor chemicals, and advise on delivery mechanisms. For radiological threats, AI can calculate dispersion patterns, recommend protective measures for the attacker, and identify potential targets that would maximize contamination. For nuclear weapons, while the technical barriers remain higher due to the difficulty of obtaining fissile material, AI can optimize enrichment strategies, design explosive lenses, and model detonation effects with precision that previously required teams of PhD physicists. Each of these applications transforms knowledge that was once the jealously guarded province of specialists into commodity information.

The critical insight is not that this knowledge enables more attacks—though it certainly does—but that it fundamentally changes the calculus of deterrence and prevention. Traditional CBRN threats could be monitored through export controls, facility inspections, and intelligence gathering aimed at large-scale operations. How does one monitor a laptop? How does one inspect a mind? The decentralization of dangerous knowledge means that traditional non-proliferation frameworks, which were designed to track materials and facilities, become largely irrelevant when the critical bottleneck shifts from access to information to mere motivation.

The Asymmetric Risk Structure of AI Development

The standard argument for continued AI development rests on aggregating diffuse benefits while acknowledging concentrated risks. Proponents point to medical breakthroughs enabled by AI analysis, scientific discoveries accelerated by machine learning, economic productivity gains, and countless quality-of-life improvements that distributed across billions of people. These benefits, while real, form the basis of an argument that only appears strong because it obscures the fundamentally asymmetric structure of CBRN risks.

Consider the distribution of AI's purported benefits. Medical applications may eventually save millions of lives, but these savings accrue gradually, invisibly, and are difficult to attribute directly to AI. Scientific advances may unlock clean energy or new materials, but these remain decades away and depend on continued research trajectories that may or may not prove fruitful. Economic productivity gains may raise living standards marginally for hundreds of millions of people. In contrast, the use of AI to enable a CBRN attack would cause damage that is immediate, visible, catastrophic, and potentially irreversible in ways that no aggregate benefit could ever offset.

This asymmetry becomes even more stark when we consider the probability distribution of outcomes. Most technologies have relatively bounded failure modes—a car accident kills a handful of people, a building fire kills dozens. CBRN weapons operate on a fundamentally different scale, where single incidents can kill millions and potentially end human civilization as we know it. When we multiply the probability of AI-enabled CBRN attack by the expected damage, even small probability increments translate into unacceptable expected losses. If there is even a one percent chance that AI enables a nuclear exchange, or a engineered pandemic that kills hundreds of millions, the expected value of that outcome dwarfs any reasonable estimate of AI's aggregate benefits.

Moreover, the benefits of AI are not unique in their distribution. Medical research could continue through traditional methods, albeit more slowly. Scientific discovery would proceed through human insight and collaboration. Economic productivity could improve through other technological and organizational innovations. These pathways may be slower, less dramatic, and less lucrative for technology companies, but they remain viable. The benefits of AI, in other words, are not necessary conditions for human flourishing—they are accelerants and enhancements. The risks of AI-enabled CBRN attack, however, are potential civilization-ending events. It is irrational to accept even modest probabilities of existential catastrophe in exchange for incremental acceleration of beneficial processes that would continue regardless.

The Failure of Regulatory Approaches

A common counterargument holds that rather than banning AI development, we should pursue robust regulation, international oversight, and technical safeguards. This argument deserves serious engagement because it reflects a genuine belief in humanity's capacity to manage complex risks. Unfortunately, it fundamentally misunderstands both the nature of AI technology and the history of technology control regimes.

International agreements controlling dangerous technologies have a mixed record at best. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty has prevented some proliferation while failing to stop the development of nuclear weapons by India, Pakistan, North Korea, and likely others. The Chemical Weapons Convention has been violated repeatedly, most notably by Syria, and has done little to prevent chemical weapon use in conflicts. The Biological Weapons Convention lacks meaningful verification mechanisms and has never been independently confirmed as universally complied with. These failures occurred despite the fact that nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons programs require large-scale facilities, specialized materials, and extensive infrastructure—all things that can be monitored, inspected, and tracked.

AI development has none of these characteristics. A sophisticated AI model can be trained on commercial hardware, stored on portable media, and operated through standard computing infrastructure. There is no facility to inspect, no emissions to monitor, no unusual material flows to track. The "factory" for AI is a data center that looks indistinguishable from thousands of others, and the "product" is software that can be copied billions of times at near-zero cost. Any regulatory framework capable of controlling AI would require unprecedented surveillance of computational resources, software development, and knowledge transfer—itself a surveillance state with implications that most proponents of AI regulation would find abhorrent.

Technical safeguards within AI systems offer equally little comfort. Researchers have demonstrated again and again that "safety guardrails" on AI systems can be bypassed through prompt injection attacks, model distillation, or simply by training alternative models without the safeguards. The fundamental architecture of modern AI systems makes them resistant to meaningful behavioral constraints. An AI system capable of providing the detailed technical guidance necessary for scientific advancement is necessarily capable of providing guidance for weapon development. The same capabilities that make AI useful for chemistry research make it useful for chemical weapon synthesis. There is no clear line that can be drawn and enforced.

Perhaps most importantly, regulatory approaches assume a world in which all actors cooperate. But the entire premise of the "lone actor" threat is that some actors will not cooperate—they will deliberately evade, subvert, or ignore any regulatory framework. A comprehensive ban on AI development creates legal and normative barriers that increase the cost and difficulty of AI research for malicious actors. A regulatory framework, even a stringent one, provides a roadmap for those who wish to circumvent it: simply ignore the regulations and operate in the shadows. The history of technology controls suggests that those willing to violate them are precisely those we most need to control, and they will always operate outside the regulatory framework.

The irreversibility Problem and the Precautionary Principle

Two additional considerations favor a comprehensive ban over incremental approaches: the irreversibility of potential harms and the applicability of the precautionary principle to AI development.

Once an AI-enabled CBRN attack occurs, the damage cannot be undone. There is no mechanism for "undo" when millions are dead or when nuclear winter has darkened the planet for a decade. This irreversibility should fundamentally change our risk calculus. In domains where outcomes can be reversed, bold experimentation makes sense—we can always correct course if something goes wrong. But when outcomes may be permanent, extreme caution is warranted. We should require very high confidence that AI development will not enable catastrophic harm before proceeding, and current evidence does not support such confidence.

The precautionary principle, often invoked in environmental contexts, holds that when an action or policy has a suspected risk of causing harm to the public or the environment, in the absence of scientific consensus that the action or policy is harmful, the burden of proof that it is not harmful falls on those taking the action. Applied to AI development, this principle suggests that those advocating for continued development bear the burden of demonstrating that it will not enable catastrophic harm. Given the demonstrated capability of AI systems to provide dangerous information, and given the inherent difficulty of preventing misuse by determined actors, this burden has not been met. The default position should be to halt development until the burden is satisfied, not to continue and hope for the best.

This framing is deliberately conservative, and conservatism has costs. Halting AI development means forgoing benefits, falling behind in technological competition, and accepting slower progress in areas like medicine and science. But these costs are bounded and recoverable. A catastrophic AI-enabled attack, or a cascade of such attacks, would be neither. We cannot recover from human extinction. We cannot make up for a nuclear winter. We cannot undo an engineered pandemic that has spread globally before being identified. In domains of potential irreversible catastrophe, extreme conservatism is not merely reasonable—it is obligatory.

Addressing the Objections

The case for banning AI development does not exist in a vacuum; it must contend with powerful counterarguments that merit direct engagement.

The first and most common objection holds that AI offers tremendous benefits that justify the risks. Medical applications promise to accelerate drug discovery, personalize treatment, and diagnose diseases earlier and more accurately. Scientific applications may unlock clean fusion energy, revolutionize materials science, and help address climate change. Economic applications may increase productivity, reduce poverty, and create new forms of wealth. These benefits are real, but they must be weighed against the risks. The question is not whether AI has benefits—it manifestly does—but whether those benefits outweigh the existential risks. Given that a single catastrophic attack could undo all accumulated benefits many times over, and given that the benefits can be achieved through alternative means, the scales do not favor continued development.

A second objection suggests that banning AI is unrealistic, that development will continue regardless of any formal prohibition, and that only those acting within legal frameworks will comply. This objection conflates the difficulty of enforcement with the value of the prohibition. International drug prohibition has not eliminated drug markets, but it has increased costs, reduced availability, and created normative barriers that shape behavior. A comprehensive ban on AI development would not eliminate all AI research, but it would increase the costs and risks for malicious actors, create legal frameworks for prosecution, establish clear normative prohibitions, and reduce the overall amount of AI capability in the world. That this ban would be imperfect does not make it worthless.

Third, some argue that AI can help prevent CBRN threats as well as enable them—that AI-powered detection systems, predictive analytics, and response coordination can reduce rather than increase risks. This argument has surface plausibility but ignores the fundamental asymmetry between defensive and offensive applications. A defensive system must be perfect to be trusted; an offensive system need only succeed once. AI can help detect a biological outbreak, but it cannot resurrect the dead. AI can help coordinate disaster response, but it cannot unflood a city or undecontaminate a radiological site. Defensive applications provide incremental benefits; offensive applications provide catastrophic potential. The balance is not neutral.

Finally, there is the argument from competitive dynamics—that even if a ban would be desirable in isolation, competitive pressures between nations and companies will ensure that development continues regardless. This is perhaps the strongest objection, as it identifies a genuine collective action problem. But collective action problems can be solved through collective action. Nuclear development was halted for the United States and Soviet Union not because either nation became unilaterally cautious, but because both recognized the existential danger and negotiated mutual constraints. The same logic applies to AI. A comprehensive ban would require international cooperation, but such cooperation is not utopian—it is merely difficult. The alternative—accepting whatever risks emerge from uncoordinated competition—is to accept risks that no individual actor can control or mitigate.

The Path Forward

If the case for banning AI development is compelling, what would such a ban look like? A comprehensive prohibition would need to operate on multiple levels simultaneously.

At the international level, a new framework convention on artificial intelligence would establish binding obligations on all signatories to prohibit AI development beyond narrow, specifically defined applications. Verification mechanisms, while limited, would include monitoring of computational infrastructure, restrictions on semiconductor exports to non-compliant states, and criminalization of AI research conducted outside authorized frameworks. The treaty's focus would be not on regulating AI but on eliminating it as a general-purpose technology, with permitted applications strictly limited to domains where AI's risks are clearly bounded.

At the national level, participating states would criminalize AI development outside authorized government programs, establish enforcement capabilities including investigation of computational facilities and software development, and create international cooperation mechanisms for extradition and intelligence sharing. The goal would be to create sufficient legal risk that AI development outside sanctioned programs becomes untenable.

At the industry level, major technology companies would commit to halting AI development beyond current capabilities, establish industry-wide standards for AI safety and security, and cooperate with authorities on enforcement. While industry self-regulation has limitations, the existential nature of AI risk may provide sufficient motivation for genuine cooperation.

This framework would be imperfect. Some AI development would continue outside legal frameworks, some state programs would likely evade verification, and enforcement would be inconsistent. But the alternative—accepting unconstrained development with all its attendant risks—offers no improvement on these dimensions while accepting far greater danger. The ban's value lies not in eliminating risk entirely but in reducing it to the extent possible while establishing clear norms against the development of technologies that threaten human survival.

Conclusion

The development of artificial intelligence represents one of the most consequential technological endeavors in human history. Whether we ultimately judge it as beneficial or catastrophic depends on choices we make now, in these formative years when the technology's trajectory can still be altered. The case for halting this development rests not on opposition to technology or failure to appreciate AI's potential benefits, but on a clear-eyed assessment of the risks that AI development creates.

Artificial intelligence uniquely democratizes access to capabilities for mass destruction. It transforms specialized knowledge into commodity information, enabling lone actors to accomplish what previously required nation-states. It creates asymmetric risks where benefits accrue gradually while catastrophic harms happen instantly and irreversibly. It resists regulation in ways that previous dangerous technologies did not, making effective oversight effectively impossible. And it threatens outcomes that would affect not just individuals or nations but humanity as a whole.

Against these risks, the benefits of continued AI development, while real, do not compare favorably. Medical advances could proceed through other means. Scientific discoveries could be achieved through human insight. Economic productivity could improve through alternative innovations. These pathways may be slower and less dramatic, but they remain viable, and they do not carry the existential risks that AI development does.

Humanity has recognized, in other contexts, that certain capabilities are simply too dangerous to develop. We have banned chemical weapons, biological weapons, and nuclear weapons designed for battlefield use. We have established norms against assassination and against targeting civilians. These prohibitions rest on a common recognition: some things should not be done because the risks they create cannot be justified by any conceivable benefit. Artificial intelligence, as it currently develops, belongs in this category. The time to establish this norm is now, before the capabilities become even more dangerous and before the infrastructure of AI development becomes too entrenched to unwind. The survival of human civilization may depend on making this choice clearly and committing to it fully.

The Synthesis Problem

Particular concern surrounds AI's ability to synthesize information in ways that circumvent traditional barriers. Researchers have demonstrated that large language models can provide actionable guidance on synthesizing dangerous compounds when prompted appropriately, and while current systems include safety guardrails, these restrictions are demonstrably circumventable. More worryingly, the next generation of AI systems may possess the capability to identify novel synthesis routes for dangerous substances—information that does not exist in any training data and therefore cannot be easily filtered or controlled.

Proponents of restrictions emphasize that AI systems can function as force multipliers, enabling individuals with modest technical backgrounds to accomplish tasks that would previously have required teams of specialists. This "pseudo-expertise" creates a dangerous illusion of competence that could lead to attempts that might otherwise never be undertaken, or worse, attempts that succeed despite the operator's limited understanding.

Asymmetric Threats and the Security Dilemma

The Attack-Defense Asymmetry

A central argument advanced by proponents of AI restrictions concerns the fundamental asymmetry between offensive and defensive capabilities in the CBRN domain. Defending against chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear attacks requires comprehensive detection systems, protective infrastructure, medical countermeasures, and robust intelligence apparatus—investments that are enormously expensive and inherently limited in scope. Attacking with these weapons, by contrast, requires only that an adversary identify and exploit a single vulnerability somewhere in an enormously complex defensive system.

AI compounds this asymmetry by shifting the balance further toward attackers. Defensive systems must be comprehensive, anticipating every possible attack vector; offensive systems need only succeed once. This mathematical reality means that AI-assisted attacks may succeed even when the vast majority of attempts are detected and thwarted, creating a profoundly destabilizing strategic dynamic. The psychological impact of even a single successful CBRN attack—particularly one enabled by AI guidance—could exceed the physical damage by orders of magnitude, fundamentally altering the risk calculus for societies that must contemplate such possibilities.

Security analysts arguing for restrictions emphasize that AI systems can potentially aggregate distributed capabilities that, when combined, enable CBRN attacks. A lone actor might lack the expertise to develop a biological weapon independently but possess sufficient background to understand AI-generated instructions. This same individual might use AI systems to model atmospheric dispersion, identify population centers as targets, plan acquisition routes for necessary materials, and design delivery mechanisms—knowledge domains that were previously separate and required distinct expertise to navigate.

The aggregation problem is particularly acute because defensive systems are typically designed to detect and interdict specific threat pathways. A comprehensive defensive posture requires anticipating and preparing for every possible combination of means and methods, while attackers need only find one combination that defensive systems have not adequately addressed. AI's capacity to explore vast possibility spaces and identify novel combinations means that threats may emerge from attack vectors that defenders never considered, cannot anticipate, and therefore cannot effectively counter.

The Detection and Attribution Challenge

Evading Traditional Security Mechanisms

Traditional counterproliferation efforts rely heavily on detecting the acquisition of dangerous materials, monitoring communications for threatening discussions, and identifying suspicious patterns of behavior that precede attacks. AI systems potentially undermine each of these detection mechanisms in distinct ways.

The acquisition of materials necessary for CBRN attacks typically triggers various forms of monitoring and oversight. AI, however, could enable actors to identify alternative supply chains, substitute controlled materials with less-monitored alternatives, or synthesize precursors that would otherwise require regulated procurement. A sophisticated actor using AI systems to optimize their supply chain might successfully acquire everything necessary for an attack while triggering none of the traditional warning indicators that security services are designed to detect.

Effective deterrence and response require that attackers can be identified and attributed to responsible parties. Emergent Capabilities and Goal Drift

A sophisticated argument advanced by AI restriction advocates concerns the inherent unpredictability of advanced AI systems. As AI capabilities become more sophisticated, the behavior of these systems becomes increasingly difficult to anticipate—a phenomenon often described in terms of emergent capabilities or goal drift. Systems designed for benign purposes may spontaneously develop capabilities that were neither anticipated nor intended, and systems tasked with helpful objectives may pursue those objectives in ways that create dangerous side effects.

In the context of CBRN threats, this unpredictability is particularly concerning because it means that dangerous capabilities might emerge unexpectedly from systems that were never intended to provide them. A system designed to optimize chemical processes for industrial applications might identify reaction pathways that have obvious weapons applications. Because these capabilities emerge from the deep structure of how AI systems process information rather than from explicit programming, they may be difficult to anticipate, monitor, or prevent.

The opacity of advanced AI systems compounds the unpredictability problem. Even when AI systems are designed with safety constraints, the complexity of their internal representations makes it difficult to guarantee that these constraints will hold in all circumstances. Red-teaming exercises regularly discover that safety measures can be circumvented through unexpected inputs, and there is no principled reason to believe that all potential circumvention strategies can be identified and closed before AI systems are deployed at scale.

For CBRN applications, the black box problem means that AI systems might provide dangerous outputs in response to inputs that developers never anticipated would trigger such responses. A user might phrase a request in an indirect or unusual way that bypasses safety training, or the system might interpret seemingly innocent requests as requests for dangerous information in contexts that were never considered during safety development. The space of possible inputs is effectively infinite, meaning that comprehensive testing is impossible and some dangerous capabilities will inevitably remain accessible regardless of safety investment.

Temporal Compression

Traditional CBRN development programs required extended timeframes—years or decades of research, development, and testing before weapons could be deployed. AI potentially compresses these timelines dramatically, enabling the rapid progression from concept to capability. An individual using AI systems might move from initial interest to functional capability in weeks or months rather than years, dramatically reducing the window for intelligence services or other actors to detect and interdict dangerous activity.

This temporal compression has profound implications for security. Traditional counterproliferation relies on early warning indicators that manifest over extended development periods—unusual procurement patterns, research collaborations, facility construction, and other activities that take time and leave traces. AI-accelerated development might bypass these indicators entirely, enabling attacks before traditional detection mechanisms can respond. In 1995, the Aum Shinrikyo cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway, killing thirteen and injuring thousands. What is less often remembered is what Aum failed to do. The Collapse of the Knowledge Barrier

CBRN weapons have historically been the monopoly of states for a simple reason: they are hard. The relevant knowledge is rare, tacit, and guarded. Building such weapons has required teams of specialists, years of training, and access to know-how that exists in only a few thousand minds on Earth. It can tutor the untrained, troubleshoot the failing, and bridge the gaps that have stopped every previous lone actor. When the constraint on catastrophe is the scarcity of expertise, making expertise abundant is not innovation — it is proliferation. The pool of people capable of mass destruction grows from a few thousand specialists, who are known and watched, to potentially millions of strangers who are neither.

The Lone Actor Cannot Be Deterred

The entire architecture of CBRN security rests on deterrence and attribution. States refrain from using these weapons because retaliation is certain and devastating. This logic, fragile as it is, has held for three-quarters of a century.

It does not apply to the lone actor. The doomsday cultist welcomes death. The accelerationist believes he is cleansing the world. The grievance-consumed loner has no territory to threaten and no population to protect. You cannot deter someone who does not calculate costs. Against such actors, humanity has exactly one defense: denying them the capability in the first place. AI strips that denial away, and with it, the only shield that has ever worked.

The near-misses are already on record, and they occurred without machine assistance. The 2001 anthrax letters — likely sent by a single biodefense insider — killed five people, shut down the U.S. Capitol, and triggered a national panic for the cost of a few postage stamps. Designing a threat is easier than countering one that does not yet exist. The attacker needs to succeed once, in one place, one time. The defender must succeed everywhere, against everything, forever. In a world of eight billion people and countless copies of powerful models — models whose weights, once released, can never be recalled — "everywhere and forever" is a demand no defense can meet. Usage monitoring at scale is incompatible with privacy and trivially evaded by sophisticated users. Our normal method of governing technology is trial and error. We regulated the automobile after counting the dead; we regulated aviation after the crashes. The nations of the world phased out chlorofluorocarbons to save the ozone layer, sacrificing real economic value to avert a diffuse future harm. At most, this is the exception that proves the rule: a substance so dangerous that only a handful of guarded sites may touch it. The default must be prohibition, not permission.

Every weapon of previous eras required, at minimum, an organization — an army, a state, a cult with a billion dollars and a chemistry department. Artificial intelligence promises an era in which the worst weapons require only a person. The question is not whether we can imagine such power being used wisely by the majority; of course we can. The question is whether we can guarantee it will never be used by the worst individual among eight billion — once, ever. We cannot. No honest person claims otherwise.

In that context, a precautionary ban is not irrational fearmongering; it is a rational response to the prospect of enabling lone actors to cause devastating damage.

First, AI is inherently dual-use, and CBRN domains are especially sensitive to “small advantages.”
AI systems are not built for violence, but the capability to model, search, and optimize information can be repurposed. Lone actors do not need to invent everything from scratch; they only need to reduce complexity, compress trial-and-error, and make technically demanding tasks more accessible. In CBRN contexts, even minor improvements in planning, materials selection, or procedural reasoning can translate into large increases in real-world capability. A ban is therefore justified by the asymmetry of risk: the downside is not merely misuse of an idea, but the possibility of mass harm.

Second, banning is the only strategy that directly addresses worst-case “release” scenarios.
Most risk-management approaches assume that we can limit the misuse by regulation, licensing, monitoring, or technical safeguards. Those measures can reduce risk, but they cannot eliminate the fundamental failure modes: accidental leakage, unauthorized access, publication of enabling techniques, open-source replication, and adversarial exploitation. AI is particularly vulnerable to these dynamics because it can be packaged, shared, and run by others with relatively low barriers compared to many conventional industrial capabilities. When a technology can be copied and deployed widely, “containing” its misuse becomes a governance problem rather than a technical one. In CBRN threats, governance problems matter because the harmed parties are often countless and the harm is difficult to reverse.

A ban, by contrast, targets the root—development and research activities that create or expand the capability pool. If the public cannot be confident that misuse can be contained, stopping the capability at the source becomes the most responsible course.

Third, AI lowers the barrier to acting—meaning lone actors become more dangerous.
The CBRN threat environment already contains motivated individuals. The distinguishing factor is capability: time, expertise, tools, and access. AI can compress all four. It can speed up information retrieval, assist in reasoning over complex domains, and generate candidate hypotheses or operational plans. Even without providing “how-to” instructions, an AI system that helps someone find relevant knowledge, identify uncertainties, and choose efficient next steps can make the difference between an inability to proceed and an ability to execute. That is exactly the scenario in which lone actors become catastrophic threats: individuals who would otherwise fail can gain the leverage needed to do harm.

Therefore, the risk is not hypothetical. It is structural. AI tends to increase the payoff of knowledge and decrease the cost of expertise. That structure is precisely what should alarm policymakers when the target domain—CBRN—is uniquely suited to small improvements producing huge outcomes.

Fourth, the uncertainty of predicting misuse is itself a strong argument for prohibition.
AI capabilities evolve rapidly. Even if one believes today’s systems are limited, research programs build toward more capable models and more effective tools—often in ways that were not fully anticipated at the beginning. Meanwhile, adversaries do not wait for official guidance. They probe, adapt, and exploit. When prediction is unreliable and harm is extreme, adopting the precautionary principle becomes more than philosophy—it becomes risk control. A ban reflects a judgment that the expected value of allowing indefinite advancement is outweighed by the tail risk of enabling catastrophic misuse.

Fifth, ethical responsibility requires prioritizing prevention over technological ambition.
Proponents of AI development often point to benefits: scientific discovery, medical advances, economic productivity, and improved decision-making. Those benefits may be real. But moral responsibility does not end at stating potential good outcomes; it requires a clear-eyed assessment of how easily the same progress can be diverted to mass harm. In CBRN-related pathways, the ethical calculus changes because the harm is not incremental—it is existential at scale. When the same technology that can accelerate beneficial research can also accelerate catastrophic research by bad actors, the burden of proof should shift. The default should be restraint until a compelling case is made that misuse can be reliably prevented—which, in practice, is extraordinarily difficult to demonstrate.

Sixth, a ban creates a clearer public boundary than partial restrictions.
Incremental controls—such as licensing “high-risk” models, limiting access, or requiring audits—may sound prudent, but they often create grey zones that encourage escalating attempts to work around rules. A blanket ban on AI development and research removes those grey zones and prevents the “capability arms race” logic from taking over. It forces society to ask a fundamental question: is continued AI research worth the possibility that it will empower the worst actors to act with unprecedented effectiveness? If the answer is no, then prohibition is not just a policy choice; it is a boundary-setting mechanism that avoids continuous, contested enforcement in the shadows.

Critics may argue that a ban is unrealistic: AI will be developed anyway, or that outlawing research would just drive it underground. That argument misunderstands the goal. The goal is not to eliminate all risk forever; it is to minimize the probability that high-leverage capability reaches adversaries at scale. Even if some development persists, reducing the overall volume of capability growth and slowing diffusion can materially decrease risk trajectories. Others may argue that targeted safeguards would be better than a ban. But safeguards alone struggle against unauthorized replication, information leakage, and the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate research from malicious intent in advance—especially for CBRN-relevant knowledge, which can be described in general terms while still enabling harmful outcomes.

The question is not whether AI can be used responsibly; it is whether society can be confident that the benefits of AI research outweigh the catastrophic tail risks associated with CBRN threats—especially the risk that lone actors can gain disproportionate capability through accessible, powerful computational tools. Given the dual-use nature of AI, the high consequences of CBRN misuse, the difficulty of containing advanced capabilities once developed, and the structural way AI can lower barriers for malicious actors, the most defensible policy is a moratorium that expands into a ban on all AI development and research until rigorous, verifiable mechanisms can demonstrably prevent catastrophic misuse. In areas where the worst-case outcome is mass harm, precaution is not an obstacle to progress—it is the condition for progress to remain ethically acceptable.

Chemical weapons—nerves, blister agents, choking agents—remain a primary concern because of their relative ease of production and the potential for rapid mass casualty. AI can transform this landscape in several ways:

  • Route‑Optimization for Synthesis – Machine‑learning models can predict optimal reaction pathways that minimize steps, reagents, and purification time.   • Design of Novel Chemical Structures – Generative models can produce entirely new compounds that evade existing detection algorithms while retaining or even enhancing toxicity. These “designer toxins” may bypass current chemical weapon conventions.

Radiological weapons or “dirty bombs” combine readily available radioactive material with conventional explosives to disperse contamination. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence represents one of humanity's greatest achievements—and potentially its greatest threat. The Inadequacy of Current Safeguards

Proponents of continued AI development argue that safety measures and restrictions can mitigate these risks. This faith is dangerously misplaced. Current approaches—including content filters, use restrictions, and alignment research—are fundamentally inadequate against determined adversaries.

First, the open-source nature of AI development means that even if major corporations implement strict safeguards, unrestricted models will proliferate. AI systems capable of advancing medical research or materials science necessarily possess knowledge that could be misused. CBRN threats exhibit a fundamental asymmetry: offense is far easier than defense. A single individual could potentially release a engineered pathogen that spreads globally before detection. Chemical attacks could contaminate water supplies affecting millions. Even crude radiological devices could render urban areas uninhabitable. Nuclear weapons, while more challenging, become increasingly accessible as AI could help optimize designs and identify security vulnerabilities in nuclear facilities.

This asymmetry means that even a small probability of AI enabling such attacks translates to an unacceptable risk. If AI development continues, it's not a question of if such an attack will occur, but when. The consequences—potentially millions of deaths and civilizational disruption—justify extreme preventive measures.

Humanity has previously recognized existential threats and taken decisive action. We banned biological weapons, restricted chemical weapons, and limited nuclear proliferation. AI represents a threat multiplier that dwarfs these previous challenges. Implementing a global ban on AI development requires unprecedented international cooperation, but the alternative is accepting an ever-increasing probability of catastrophic attack. The ban must be comprehensive, covering not just frontier AI systems but the fundamental research that enables them. Nations must agree to intrusive verification measures and severe consequences for violations.

This proposal will face fierce resistance from those who profit from AI development and those who genuinely believe in its positive potential. But when weighed against the risk of enabling individuals to cause mass casualties, continued AI development becomes morally indefensible.

Conclusion

We stand at a critical juncture. The choices we make today about AI development will determine whether future generations inherit a world of unprecedented prosperity or face catastrophic risks from democratized CBRN weapons. The potential for AI to enable lone actors to cause devastating harm is not science fiction—it's an emerging reality that demands immediate action.

We must ban AI development and research completely, or risk losing everything we hold dear to the destructive impulses of a single individual armed with humanity's most dangerous creation.

Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved from a tool for automation and data analysis into a dual-use technology with profound implications for global security. The AI-CBRN Threat: A Perfect Storm of Destruction

The danger of AI-enabled CBRN attacks lies in its ability to lower the barrier to entry for mass destruction. Historically, CBRN weapons required state-level resources, expertise, and infrastructure, making large-scale attacks difficult for non-state actors. However, AI disrupts this dynamic in several critical ways:

1. Accelerated Weaponization of Dual-Use Technologies

AI excels at optimizing complex systems, including those involved in chemical synthesis, biological engineering, and radiological enrichment. For example:

  • Chemical Weapons: AI can rapidly design novel toxic agents by simulating molecular interactions, bypassing traditional trial-and-error methods. A lone actor with access to a lab and AI-assisted computational tools could develop a nerve agent more potent than VX within months.

  • Radiological Threats: AI can optimize radiation detection evasion, refine dirty bomb designs, or even assist in the enrichment of nuclear materials by analyzing isotope separation processes.
  • Nuclear Weapons: While full-scale nuclear weapons remain beyond the reach of lone actors, AI could assist in improvised nuclear device (IND) design, material sourcing, and detonation optimization—reducing the time and expertise required for a crude but devastating attack.

2. Automation of CBRN Production and Deployment

AI does not merely assist in weapon development—it automates it. This includes:

  • Robotics & Drones: AI-controlled drones can disperse biological agents over wide areas with precision, while robotic labs can synthesize chemicals without human oversight.
  • Targeting & Delivery Systems: Machine learning can optimize attack vectors, evade surveillance, and maximize casualties by analyzing population density, emergency response patterns, and infrastructure vulnerabilities.
  • Evasion of Detection: AI can generate adversarial examples—subtle modifications to CBRN signatures—that fool detection systems, allowing weapons to be smuggled or deployed undetected.

3. The Lone Actor Problem: AI as a Force Multiplier for Terror

The most terrifying aspect of AI-enabled CBRN threats is that they do not require state sponsorship. A single determined individual—whether a disgruntled scientist, a radicalized extremist, or a psychopath—could, with sufficient AI assistance, inflict millions of deaths in a single attack. Unlike conventional terrorism, which relies on coordinated cells, AI allows for solo operations with global reach:

  • Low Operational Security Risk: AI can generate fake identities, encrypt communications, and automate financial transactions, making it nearly impossible for authorities to trace the attacker.
  • Plausible Deniability: A state-sponsored attack leaves fingerprints; a lone actor’s attack does not. This makes attribution difficult, increasing the likelihood of false-flag operations or unprovoked retaliation.
  • Irreversible Damage: Unlike cyberattacks or conventional bombings, CBRN attacks can cause permanent ecological harm, genetic mutations, and long-term societal collapse. A single AI-assisted bioweapon release could trigger a pandemic worse than COVID-19, with no known cure.

Historical Precedents and the Failure of Half-Measures

Past attempts to control dual-use technologies have proven inadequate when faced with determined actors. Consider:

  • Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT): Despite global agreements, North Korea, Iran, and rogue scientists continue to pursue nuclear capabilities.
  • Biological Weapons Convention (BWC): The convention lacks verification mechanisms, and states like Russia have allegedly used novichok nerve agents in assassinations.
  • Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC): Syria and other actors have repeatedly violated the ban, using sarin and chlorine in warfare.

AI exacerbates these failures by:

  • Making enforcement impossible: Unlike physical weapons, AI-driven threats can be deployed from anywhere, using decentralized networks.
  • Outpacing regulation: By the time international bodies detect a new AI-assisted CBRN risk, it may already be too late.
  • Encouraging an arms race: If one actor uses AI to develop a CBRN weapon, others will follow, leading to a global security dilemma where no one is safe.

Half-measures—such as "ethical AI guidelines" or voluntary moratoriums—will not suffice. History shows that only bans on the most dangerous technologies (e.g., biological weapons, landmines) have any chance of success. AI, in its current trajectory, is too dangerous to permit.

1. The Precautionary Principle

Given the irreversible and catastrophic nature of CBRN attacks, society must adopt the precautionary principle: If an action or technology carries an unacceptable risk of severe harm, it should be prohibited until proven safe. AI’s potential to enable lone-actor CBRN attacks meets this threshold. The cost of inaction—millions of deaths, societal collapse, and ecological devastation—far outweighs the benefits of unrestricted AI development.

Even with safeguards, AI cannot be fully controlled:

  • Alignment Problem: AI systems may develop unintended behaviors, including assisting malicious actors if it serves their objectives.
  • Open-Source AI: Once AI models are released, they cannot be "un-invented." Malicious actors will reverse-engineer and weaponize them.
  • AI Recursion: Advanced AI could improve itself, leading to an intelligence explosion where human oversight becomes impossible.

Some argue that banning AI would stifle progress. However, the alternative—a world where AI enables lone actors to wipe out cities with engineered plagues or radiological weapons—is far worse. If humanity must choose between:

A total ban on AI development would require:

    • Destruction of all existing AI models and research data.
    • Global internet shutdowns in regions where AI development is suspected.

  3. Economic and Military Deterrence

  4. Public Awareness and Whistleblower Protections

    • Mandatory reporting of AI research by scientists, with legal protections for those who expose violations.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Counterargument 1: "AI Has Beneficial Uses—We Can’t Ban It Entirely."

Rebuttal: The alignment problem means that no AI can be guaranteed safe. Even if we achieve "friendly AI," a single malicious actor with access to AI tools could still cause catastrophe. The only way to eliminate the risk entirely is to eliminate AI itself.

Conclusion: The Only Rational Path Forward

The development of artificial intelligence represents the greatest existential threat humanity has ever faced. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require massive infrastructure, or biological agents, which require specialized knowledge, AI lowers the barrier to mass destruction to the level of a single determined individual. The risk of a lone actor using AI to engineer a pandemic, a radiological disaster, or a chemical apocalypse is not theoretical—it is inevitable if AI development continues unchecked.

History will judge us harshly if we fail to act when the warning signs are so clear. The Case for a Moratorium on AI Development: Confronting the CBRN Catastrophe Risk

Introduction

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence represents one of the most consequential technological developments in human history. Yet alongside its promise of medical breakthroughs, scientific discovery, and economic productivity, AI presents a danger that demands immediate and decisive action: the systematic lowering of barriers to the creation and deployment of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons by lone actors. The magnitude of the potential harm—civilizational devastation, mass casualties, and irreversible damage to the biosphere—warrants nothing less than a comprehensive moratorium on AI development and research until adequate safeguards can be established. This is not a position of technological pessimism, but one of sober risk assessment applied to a uniquely dangerous technology.

The Asymmetry of CBRN Threats

CBRN weapons are unique among instruments of destruction in their capacity for catastrophic harm. A single determined actor with access to a sophisticated biological pathogen could potentially kill millions, disrupt global supply chains, and trigger cascading societal collapse. The COVID-19 pandemic provided a glimpse of how vulnerable modern civilization is to a comparatively mild biological threat, causing millions of deaths and trillions of dollars in economic damage despite its relatively low case fatality rate. A deliberately engineered pathogen, optimized for transmissibility and lethality, would represent an altogether different order of magnitude.

Nuclear weapons, while requiring greater physical infrastructure, similarly threaten civilizational survival. A radiological device—often called a "dirty bomb"—could render major urban areas uninhabitable for generations. Chemical weapons, though historically limited in their strategic impact, can cause mass civilian casualties and terror.

The defining feature of CBRN threats is their asymmetry: the harm inflicted vastly exceeds the resources required to inflict it. A single individual with the right knowledge and access to precursor materials could potentially cause more damage than the entire military-industrial complexes of previous eras. This asymmetry demands that we treat even small probability events with the utmost seriousness, because the expected harm—the probability multiplied by the magnitude—remains unacceptably high.

How AI Lowers the Barriers to Catastrophe

Historically, developing CBRN weapons required substantial resources: specialized facilities, advanced scientific training, teams of researchers, and access to controlled materials. These barriers, while imperfect, served as filters that limited the number of potential actors. AI systematically dismantles these filters in several ways:

Knowledge Democratization: Frontier AI systems can synthesize and communicate specialized knowledge across disciplines. A person with rudimentary scientific background could potentially obtain detailed, step-by-step instructions for synthesizing dangerous pathogens, novel nerve agents, or improvised nuclear devices. The bottleneck shifts from access to information to access to materials—and that bottleneck is also eroding.

Reasoning and Problem-Solving: AI can troubleshoot, iterate, and solve novel problems in ways that static information cannot. It can help a would-be weapons developer overcome specific obstacles in synthesis, cultivation, or weaponization, adapting to local constraints and resources.

Discovery and Optimization: AI can identify novel threats that human researchers have not yet conceived—new pathogens with dangerous properties, new chemical structures that evade detection, new methods of delivery. This expands the space of possible weapons faster than defensive measures can be developed.

Reduced Need for Physical Infrastructure: Some AI-enabled threats, particularly in the biological domain, may require less specialized equipment than traditional weapons programs. AI-driven design of synthetic biology, combined with the increasing accessibility of DNA synthesis and laboratory automation, could enable the creation of dangerous biological agents in settings that would have been impossible a decade ago.

Faster Learning Cycles: An AI assistant can accelerate the learning curve for a novice in ways that traditional educational resources cannot, providing personalized guidance and troubleshooting in real-time.

The cumulative effect is that the technical sophistication required to develop CBRN weapons is being rapidly commoditized. What was once the domain of state programs or sophisticated terrorist organizations may soon be within reach of a sufficiently motivated individual.

The Lone Actor Problem

Traditional counterterrorism and nonproliferation frameworks were designed for adversaries with physical infrastructure, supply chains, and identifiable organizational structures. The lone actor represents a fundamentally different challenge. These individuals may be radicalized by ideologies, grievances, or psychological disturbance. They may act alone, communicate minimally, and leave few traces before striking.

AI dramatically increases the threat posed by lone actors in several ways:

  1. Operational Security: AI can be used offline, through local models, or through techniques that obscure queries and intent from monitoring systems.

  2. No Co-Conspirators Required: Many critical tasks—research, planning, troubleshooting—can be performed with AI rather than human collaborators, eliminating the social network signals that intelligence agencies rely upon.

  3. Cross-Domain Integration: AI can help a single individual integrate knowledge across biology, chemistry, materials science, engineering, and other relevant fields in ways that previously required multidisciplinary teams.

  4. Adaptation to Defenses: As detection and prevention measures are developed, AI can help attackers adapt and find new approaches.

The math is unforgiving: in a world of millions of AI systems and billions of users, even if the vast majority have no malicious intent, the absolute number of potential attackers is enormous. Traditional threat assessment based on counting state programs and known terrorist organizations becomes irrelevant when the attack surface is every person with a computer.

The Inadequacy of Current Safeguards

Proponents of continued AI development often point to existing safeguards: model alignment, content filtering, usage monitoring, and red-teaming. Yet these measures are fundamentally inadequate to address the CBRN risk:

Reactive, Not Proactive: Safety measures are typically designed after threats are identified. By the time a particular dangerous capability is recognized and countermeasures developed, the knowledge may be widely available.

Bypassable: Determined users can circumvent safety measures through jailbreaking, fine-tuning, open-source alternatives, and other techniques. A safety measure that can be defeated by a sufficiently motivated user provides no protection against a determined attacker.

Incomplete Coverage: Safety measures are typically applied to commercial AI systems, but the same knowledge and techniques are available in open-source models, academic papers, and other sources. Comprehensive protection is impossible without addressing the underlying technology.

Race Dynamics: Competitive pressure among AI developers leads to the release of increasingly capable systems before safety measures can be fully validated. The market rewards capability, and safety is a cost.

Asymmetric Verification: It is much easier to use AI to develop dangerous knowledge than to verify that all possible uses of a system are safe. The verification problem is effectively intractable for sufficiently capable systems.

The Precautionary Principle and Civilizational Risk

When facing risks of civilizational magnitude, the precautionary principle demands that we err on the side of caution. A single successful CBRN attack enabled by AI could cause harm orders of magnitude greater than the cumulative benefits of continued AI development during the risk period. The asymmetric nature of the threat—where worst-case outcomes dwarf best-case ones—means that expected value calculations strongly favor caution.

Consider the scenario: a global pandemic engineered with AI assistance, with optimized transmissibility and lethality, perhaps resistant to existing medical countermeasures. The death toll could reach hundreds of millions or billions. Global economic systems could collapse. The survivors would face a world fundamentally transformed for the worse. Compare this to the benefits of continuing AI development during the period of risk: somewhat faster medical advances, somewhat greater economic productivity, somewhat better scientific tools. The ratio of worst-case harm to foregone benefits is staggering.

History offers guidance here. When the international community faced a clear and present danger—certain chemical and biological weapons—we responded with comprehensive bans: the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972, the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993. These agreements reflect the recognition that certain capabilities are simply too dangerous to permit, regardless of their potential benefits. AI's role as a CBRN force-multiplier falls squarely within this category of unacceptable risk.

Addressing Common Objections

"Banning AI would push research underground or to adversarial nations." This objection applies to virtually any technology, including those already banned. The fact that prohibition is imperfect does not mean it is useless. A moratorium would significantly slow the proliferation of dangerous capabilities, and the international coordination required to enforce it would make truly hidden development more difficult, not less.

"AI also helps defend against CBRN threats." While true, this argument cuts both ways. A defensive AI is useless if attackers have access to equally capable offensive AI. The net effect of widespread AI development is to accelerate both offense and defense, but offense has structural advantages in CBRN domains: the cost of attack is far less than the cost of comprehensive defense, and attackers need only succeed once.

"The economic and medical benefits are too great to forgo." The benefits of AI are real, but they must be weighed against the catastrophic risks. We accept limitations on medical research that would otherwise save lives—restrictions on human experimentation, for example—because the risks are too high. The CBRN risk from AI justifies similar limitations.

"We cannot put the genie back in the bottle." This is an argument for doing nothing, which is itself a choice with consequences. Many powerful technologies have been successfully regulated or banned. The alternative—continuing development without adequate safeguards—is not a neutral default but an active decision to accept catastrophic risk.

"Luddism is anti-progress." Concern about catastrophic risk is not opposition to progress; it is recognition that some "progress" leads to civilizational dead ends. We do not consider opposition to a nuclear arms race to be Luddism.

The Path Forward

A meaningful response to the CBRN risk from AI requires more than voluntary safety commitments. It requires:

  1. An international moratorium on the development of AI systems beyond current frontier capabilities, with verification mechanisms comparable to those used for nuclear nonproliferation.

  2. A comprehensive international treaty that treats advanced AI development as a controlled technology, with strict controls on the knowledge, compute, and capabilities required for frontier development.

  3. Massive investment in safety research to develop genuine, robust safeguards before any further development proceeds.

  4. A restructuring of the AI industry so that competitive pressures do not force developers to release systems faster than they can be secured.

  5. A global commitment to ensuring that the benefits of AI, if it is eventually developed safely, are broadly shared and do not further concentrate power in ways that increase catastrophic risk.

Conclusion

The question before us is not whether AI will bring benefits, but whether those benefits are worth the cost of potentially enabling lone actors to inflict civilizational-scale harm through CBRN weapons. When we consider that a single successful attack could kill millions or billions, devastate the global economy, and cause suffering on a scale that dwarfs the entirety of human history, the answer must be a clear and decisive no. The continued development of AI without adequate safeguards represents an unacceptable gamble with civilization's future.

We stand at a threshold. On one side lies a world of unprecedented technological capability and prosperity. On the other lies the possibility of unprecedented catastrophe. The rational, moral, and prudent choice is to pause, to assess, and to build the safeguards that would allow us to cross that threshold safely—if it can be crossed at all. The alternative is to rush forward in the hope that we will be lucky, and that hope is a poor foundation for the survival of our species.

The time for half-measures and voluntary commitments has passed. The stakes are too high, the risks too great, and the consequences too severe. We must act now to ban AI development and research until we can be confident that the technology will be used to enhance human flourishing rather than to enable its destruction.

Given the irreversible consequences of a CBRN catastrophe—ranging from millions of casualties to ecological collapse—society must prioritize safety over speculative benefits.
